text: Centralizing logs in one searchable place is useful, and plenty of tools do it well. But storing and searching logs is not the same thing as running a SIEM, and the two get confused constantly -- in vendor marketing, in job postings, and in how teams describe their own setup. The real difference comes down to what happens after the logs land: does anything watch them in real time, or does a human have to go looking?

A log management tool's whole job is two steps: centralize logs from wherever they come from, and let someone search them. That's genuinely valuable -- an application crashes, and an analyst searches across every server's logs for the matching stack trace in seconds instead of connecting into each box individually. But the tool itself isn't watching for anything. It waits to be asked.

A SIEM starts from that same centralized foundation and adds three things log management doesn't have: correlation rules that run continuously and automatically across every source, alerting that notifies an analyst the moment a rule fires -- without anyone searching first -- and security-specific analytics, like matching activity against threat intelligence feeds, built for detecting attacks rather than general troubleshooting.

Picture the same environment running both. With log management alone, nothing happens until a human decides to look -- an app crashes, and someone searches the stack trace. With a SIEM watching the same logs, five failed logins across three different systems inside five minutes gets correlated and raises an alert on its own, before any analyst thought to go searching for it. That automatic, unasked-for detection is the entire difference.

That's also why the distinction matters beyond terminology: a tool that only centralizes and searches logs is log management, no matter how good its search is, and calling it a SIEM overstates what a team actually has in place. Next lesson surveys the platforms that actually do this in production -- Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, and the Elastic Stack -- and what each one is genuinely known for.
